title: Better for whom?: why "we'll build it better" is never a valid business idea
summary: Jason argues that "better" has no meaning without a specific market segment, so "we can do it better" is not a real idea for a business. Defining who your product is better for turns a vague claim into an actual proposal. It also tells you how to advertise, what to build, and who to interview.

principles.text: "We can do it better" is never a valid business idea; "better" only exists for a specific market segment.
principles.quote: You quickly realize there's no such thing as "better."  There's only such thing as "better for a specific market segment."

principles.text: Always ask "better for whom?" when a founder claims their product is better than the incumbents.
principles.quote: So when someone says their product is "better," my next question is always: "Better for whom?"

principles.text: A real pitch defines "better" by naming the audience and the use-case the incumbents serve poorly.
principles.quote: at least they are *actual ideas,* actual proposals, in that they *define* "better:"

principles.text: Naming your audience tells you how to advertise, where to go, what words to use, and what features to build.
principles.quote: If you know your audience, you can create targeted advertisements, go to specific conferences, and even cold-call them on LinkedIn.

principles.text: Knowing who it's better for gives you the basis for customer development: who to call and what to verify.
principles.quote: Or if you're still in the ideation stage, it gives you the basis for [customer development](https://longform.asmartbear.com/customer-development/), both in finding potential customers to call, and what you're verifying when you get them on the phone.

principles.text: Differentiate against crowded markets by picking an underserved segment, such as beginners, complex projects, or mobile-first users.
principles.quote: My PM tool is best for large, complex projects with modern technology requirements.
